item.title: Come to Brazil
item.description: Tyler Cowen tries the world’s third best Italian food
item.content:encoded:
By Works in Progress

In this article from Issue 26, Tyler Cowen argues you should go to Brazil.

One of my joys in traveling to Brazil, which I did recently for the seventh time, is dining. In general, Latin America is the great underdiscovered frontier for top-tier food. Most of the region is undertouristed, affordable, and not – yet? – obsessed with Instagramming what arrives on the plate. And Brazil is one of the peaks in the region.

With the possible exception of Uruguay and also Kobe, Japan, Brazil has in my not-so-humble opinion the best beef. Of the very finest steak meals I have had, two of the top three were in southern Brazil.

The basics of the Brazilian countryside, and Brazilian agriculture, make such successes possible. Brazil has plenty of space, lots of fertile land, and high agricultural productivity, all combined with relatively short supply chains. That combination means that the foodstuffs are plentiful and fresh.

Most of all, the Brazilian dining achievements are a progress story. Often Brazilian yields in agriculture are approaching those of the United States, or they are occasionally superior, even though Brazil is a much poorer country. Brazil has done a remarkably good job integrating technology into its food sector, though sadly most of the rest of the economy has not followed suit.

Brazil also is a nation of immigrants. Brazil has roughly two million citizens of Japanese origin – there is no exact figure – most of them living in the south. Brazil is thus one of the best places, after Japan itself, to enjoy Japanese food.

In June this year I patronized an omakase restaurant in São Paulo, Kan Suke, which has been awarded one Michelin star. I had a fifteen-course omakase for $110, with personal service from the head chef. Only eight seats. I reserved a mere half hour in advance, a difficult feat to pull off in comparable restaurants elsewhere. All the other diners seemed to be Brazilian Japanese, which added to the cultural flair of the experience.

Brazil also has about 30 million citizens of Italian descent, the largest such diaspora in the world. I recently had a debate with a very well-traveled Italian friend of mine, from foodie haven Modena, and we concluded that Brazil is the third-best country in the world for Italian food, after Italy itself and then Japan.

If you are into fruit, Brazil has much to offer. A list of some starter options would include acai, cupuaçu, caju (‘cashew apple’), soursop, bacaba, jabuticaba, pitanga, cambuci, pequi, umbu (Brazil plum), mangaba, and others. Nor should you neglect the less exotic items. When I took my daughter to Brazil for the first time, she remarked simply ‘I have never had a banana before.’ A special favorite of mine is hearts of palm (not technically a fruit), which in Brazil have a sweetness and texture reminiscent of sushi.

Brazil, like most large nations, also offers multiple cuisines. For instance you can go to Minas Gerais for pork and beans. Minas beans would be my favorite of what I have sampled, surpassing Mexico. Belem serves cuisine from the Amazon region, including exotic river fish, dried shrimp, duck, and rice, with flavors from cassava, manioc, and the local fruit. You cannot get those dishes in many other places.

Feijoada is of slave origins, and is often associated with Rio de Janeiro, but it has evolved into a national dish, available almost everywhere. Think rice, black beans, collard greens, orange slices, and farofa, a kind of manioc flour, with different parts of the pig mixed in. At home I cook the vegetarian version of this dish. The coolness and sweetness of the orange go well with the sandy texture of the farofa, and the meal hardly costs anything to make.

Rio de Janeiro offers highly cosmopolitan options, and the city has a tradition of excellent French and Continental restaurants.

The best churrascarias I have had were on the outskirts of Curitiba in the south. You can get an excellent pasta meal combined with your choice of many kinds of meat, leading to an impossibly large quantity of food at your disposal. I favored these establishments more in my youth, but if you have never tried them, you are missing something.

Campo Grande, the booming agro-city in central western Brazil, has a derivative form of Okinawan soba (!) as a dining specialty. I regret that, due to a delayed flight connection, I have yet to try this apparent delicacy.

Desserts are very traditionally Western and European. They lack originality but are high in quality and consistent in execution. For chocolate ice cream and gelato, favorites of mine, the country is top tier.

I can’t say I find all of the food in Brazil underrated. You will hear lavish praise for the dishes from the northeast, specifically the heavy coconut milk and palm oil blends, sometimes coming under the name moqueca. I suspect some of these meals are wonderful in the more rural parts of the Northeast, but when I have tried them in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and also Salvador, they struck me as mucky, lacking clarity of flavor, and too heavy to boot. The fault might be mine in the selection of restaurants, but practically speaking I think you have to work hard to get fine food from this regional cuisine.

São Paulo is the dining capital of Brazil, and as a highly commercial, business-oriented city it offers dishes from all the major regions of the country. It also attracts very few tourists. During my four-day trip there I wandered plenty, including to a variety of parks and museums, and I saw only a few people who obviously were foreign tourists. That helps keep an integrity to the dining scene, since most of the restaurants are geared toward regular customers who know local food reputations well.

As for price, the restaurants are not dirt cheap, as you might find in parts of Mexico and Southeast Asia. Still, even in São Paulo they are much less expensive than in New York, Paris, or London, and at the upper end of the market you will find comparably high standards of décor and service.

Brazil is not a country where you need to resort to street food, unless we are talking sandwiches. The offerings in restaurants are authentic enough, so you do not need to go ‘slumming’ to get the real thing. You may find that either a plus or a minus.

In the meantime, the demands on your time and attention just got more complicated.

Tyler Cowen is an economist.

item.title: Young prudes
item.content:encoded:
By Aria Schrecker

January 2022. TikTok had chosen its villain of the week. West Elm Caleb was a six-foot-four mustachioed lothario who had strung along several different women. They took to TikTok to tell their matching stories of being made Spotify mixtapes and then being ghosted and were outraged to discover a pattern. He became an avatar for hitherto suppressed rage as people uncovered his precise identity and tried to get him fired. A dating app even took out a billboard about him.

Cads are nothing new. What was new is that these women felt they had been morally wronged. In millennial culture, ‘fuckboys’ are generally considered to be an amoral force of nature, the bridge trolls you pay to participate in 2010s sex positivity. The view from the Huffington-Post-iverse was that they were probably better people than the so-called nice guys who can’t get laid. The kids have a different view. Polling says that young people today are less likely to have sex on a first date or a one-night stand, and are more interested in marriage.

Subscribe to print

The younger generation’s reaction against casual sex has puzzled older commentators. Much like the rise of the New Right, the arc of history was not meant to bend like this. But the rise of prudishness was to be expected. From the Second World War, up to the 1990s, American dating markets had too many women. I think this is a partial explanation for why the sexual revolution happened. Now, they have too many men.

The standard story of the sexual revolution is that we invented the contraceptive pill, unleashed it upon the white-picket-fence nuclear families of postwar America, and – depending on your politics – either liberated or destroyed them with sex, drugs, and rock ‘n’ roll.

It’s a neat story, but it doesn’t quite fit the facts. By the time the pill was approved in 1960, premarital sex had been on a steady, multi-decade rise in America. By 1953, half of women reported having had premarital sex. And contraception is popular in lands untouched by the sexual revolution. Condoms, the pill and sterilization are all widely available in India, but only 3 percent of unmarried women will admit to having had sex. Abortion and contraception have been widely practiced in Japan since the 1950s, but they still haven’t had a pro-casual sex revolution either.

At the start of the early twentieth century, middle and upper class courtship was managed by an arcane system of courting etiquette and socially filtered matchmaking by elders. Most people in Western culture expected to marry for love, but male-female socializing was chaperoned, and respectable young women were only introduced to men within their social class. This changed in the roaring twenties as dating trickled up from the working classes, who moved to cities for work and didn’t have their mothers around to issue invitations or parlors to host in.

Subscribe now

When dating first arose, America had too many men. Mass immigration meant that in 1920 there were 104 men for every 100 women. So for dating’s first two decades, women had the upper hand. Men took them out dancing, paid for their milkshakes, and everyone got married a little younger. Free from parental watchfulness some ‘necking and petting’ was known to happen, and the amount of premarital sex rose, but it remained a minority pursuit rather than an expectation.

After the Second World War, for the first time in its history, the United States had surplus women. Because couples consistently opt for relationships where the man is slightly older, a high birth rate can create a false shortage of men. From the end of the Second World War until 1961 every cohort of babies was bigger than the one before: 3.7 million were born in 1950, 3.8 million in 1951, and 3.9 in 1952. The average age gap between couples was two years meaning there were only 1.85 million boys born in 1950 for the 1.95 million girls born in 1952, creating an oversupply of 105 women for every 100 men a couple of years older than them. So from the 1940s through to the 1990s, Americans experienced a dating market with a false shortage of men.

Even before we had reliable contraception, the number of women having premarital sex tripled. Only one in seven women from the 1920s had sex before marriage. Half the youth of 1950 did. Of course, sex without commitment or reliable contraception could have been devastating but shotgun marriages rose substantially. A sixth of first borns to married couples in the early 1960s were the product of premarital shenanigans (versus a twelfth in 1920).

The male shortage had a big impact on Asian marriage markets too. In India, dowries (payments from the bride’s family to the groom’s) rose in the decades following the Baby Boom, tripling from 1930 to 1975. Now sex selective abortion has inverted the sex ratio – there are 13.5 million 24-year-old men for the 12.3 million 19-year-old women – and so, running counter to the long tradition of dowries bride buying has become a problem in the most sex-skewed parts of India.

Similarly, the arranged-marriage-based ultra-Orthodox Jewish community in the United States grows by about four percent a year, leading to what they call a ‘shidduch crisis’ (shidduch being the name for their system of matchmaking). For every 100 men who are 22, they have 112 women who are 19. Nose jobs are becoming a popular present for girls before they get matched. Tellingly, the Hasidic parts of the community, where men and women typically enter shidduch at the same age, have no similar crisis.

Subscribe to print

The cleanest evidence comes from college campuses, which provide us with hundreds of micro dating markets with wildly different sex ratios. Women on more female-skewed college campuses go on fewer dates and are less likely to have a boyfriend but more likely to be sexually active. They also think less of men.

Perhaps, having cooked up a theory, I’m just seeing it everywhere. I’m overinterpreting stats like they’re a Rorschach test. But the data lines up. Birth rates in America rose up to 1961, giving us increasing sexual liberty up to the 1990s. Then, up to the mid-2000s, they fluctuated around four million a year, giving us stable norms up to the 2010s. After that, birth rates fell from the mid-2000s onward. For current young people, that means there are 104 20-year-old men for every 100 18-year-old women. Effectively, we’re back to the pre-War gender skew.

Just like the 1960s, we’re headed for society-wide upheaval as we renegotiate sexual norms. Teenagers post viral videos shaming adults canoodling in the park, calling them disgusting and asking that they ‘think of the children’. Why Men Love Bitches, an early 2000s dating manual encouraging women to demand higher standards, has returned to the book charts after going viral on TikTok. The ‘Sprinkle Sprinkle’ method is a new dating trend that encourages women to use men for their money; girls who participate brag about their boyfriends paying the deposit on their apartments and about laughing if a man tries to split the bill on a date.

We’re already seeing a decrease in sex (casual or otherwise), which a lot of people attribute to smartphones. I think soon we’ll see people getting married sooner too. It’s only a matter of time before a West Elm Caleb-style reckoning comes for a man who drags his feet on proposing to his girlfriend. It’s happening in fits and starts, but I see a return to 1930s dating on the horizon.

Aria Schrecker is an editor at Works in Progress.

Join us on December 3rd at the London School of Economics. RSVP here.

Britain struggles to build almost anything: houses, infrastructure, data centres, and everything else. Its economy is anaemic. It has the most expensive energy of almost anywhere in the world. Its labour market looks dangerously exposed to shocks to professional services. The British state is paralysed and unable to act.

​Two years ago, when we published Foundations: Why Britain has stagnated, these were important facts for anyone who cared about reviving Britain’s economy. Today, they will decide whether Britain thrives in the age of AI or goes the way of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and twentieth century Argentina.

​You are invited to join us at Building Abundance: How Britain can flourish in the age of AI, a day of ideas for rebuilding Britain’s economy and state so it can adapt to and embrace artificial intelligence and other opportunities for growth.

​It will be held on Thursday 3rd December at the London School of Economics, from 1pm to 7:30pm (doors open 1pm for a 1:20pm start). This is hosted by Works in Progress in association with the LSE Law School and School of Public Policy. Tickets are free.

​Our keynote sessions feature former Prime Ministerial advisors Dominic Cummings and Morgan McSweeney in conversation on the decline and fall of British state capacity, and John Fingleton on what the government has and has not done to put his review of nuclear regulation into effect, one year after committing to implement it in full.

item.title: Against supplements
item.content:encoded:
By Ben Southwood

This column was featured in Issue 26. Subscribe today to get Issue 27, arriving early next month, and an issue every two months thereafter, delivered straight to your home or workplace.

‘You just piss it oot,’ my friend Stuart Ritchie has always told me. In a politer register, other friends have expressed scepticism too. But for a long time, despite the wisdom of my smartest scientist pals, I was an enthusiastic believer in supplementation. As recently as five years ago, I had a long list of supplements I recommended for normal people, based on my research. I no longer take anything and haven’t for a while, and I don’t think there is an especially good case for anyone to do so without having a specific justification, like bloodwork or the advice of a doctor.

Subscribe to print

My thinking in my supplement era was simple: there is no special reason to think everyone’s diets are giving them an optimal amount of every micro- or phytonutrient. It might be that the perfect amount is some way above the threshold for not being deficient. Therefore, I argued, with the right evidence it was worth punting on various supplements, like choline, vitamin K2 (menaquinones 4 and 7, naturally), fish oil or omega-3 fatty acids (prepared in the right way, of course), and potentially many more things. I took wheat germ (for its spermine and spermidine). I even took glycine, a slightly sweet amino acid prominent in skin and bone but not muscle meat, which people online claim improves their sleep.

I was an evangelist. My wild-eyed confidence and thorough research inspired many people over the years to take one thing or another that I recommended on my ever-permuting list. I had an easy audience, because there seems to be a near-universal drive toward supplementation, either as a kind of inherited folk memory of beriberi, pellagra, scurvy, and rickets, or perhaps as a natural human instinct – the same one that makes us want a pill when we leave the doctor’s office.

My method was tripartite. I reasoned that though we can’t be absolutely sure, a supplement was, on balance, likely worth taking if three things held. First, we have a plausible evolutionary story about how we originally evolved in an environment with more of it, and our modern diets do not. Second, there is a logical, not obviously disputed, story about how it works. Third, the balance of evidence suggests that consuming the nutrient at least correlates with good health, and ideally well-designed trials show that it actually causes good health.

With such a rigorous method, how did everything fall apart? It’s a sad story. Ultimately, it was both a bad methodology and I applied it badly. The core problem is the same problem for all theorizing, the same problem the methodology of science was designed to solve: it is very easy to validate one’s tender hypotheses by looking carefully for validating evidence. Another perhaps equally big problem is that most science is nearly useless.

Let’s start with the first problem. Basically, I have an underlying psychological... call it a trait rather than a flaw, though there is a case for either name. This psychological trait makes me take pleasure in having bespoke, rare, fresh, interesting opinions. You might call it metacontrarianism. I love to have original views, and it’s possible, I admit, that I get just a little bit invested in these opinions and in proving that they are right.

Subscribe now

Now, this combines with another trait I have, this one definitely a flaw: food obsessiveness. I’m afraid that I was a pathologically, distressingly fussy child who would eat only a handful of plain foods. As a teenager, I forwent artificial colorings and flavorings completely, to an extent that made people think (rightly) that I was a freak. For years, I ate only during a six-hour window between 2pm and 8pm. At other times, I have obsessively counted calories, or completely avoided carbs. Currently, I just eat a lot of fiber. I follow dietary fads like I am constantly switching religions.

This naturally led me to search out evidence that would allow me to believe, with at least some reason, that we are short on vitamin K2 because our diet is lower in liver, alpine cheese, and grass-fed butter. My elegant evolutionary story combined with a plausible mechanism for how K2 would help us – preventing arterial calcification brought on by a diet with too much calcium – and with evidence that adults with more vitamin K2 are healthier. There are even academic studies showing that vitamin K2 improves health. Voila: I began taking a specific brand of vitamin K2 supplement (InnovixLabs Full Spectrum), which I judged to have the right balance of the rarer menaquinone-4 (this word on its own has a certain ring to internet users of the early 2010s) and the less rare menaquinone-7.

And so on for the other supplements. I had complex views on which ones were dangerous (copper), which were pointless (B vitamins except B12; creatine in omnivores), and which were essential (K2 menaquinone-4). This complexity was a great deal of what made the whole thing so enjoyable, akin to being into a fandom like Warhammer with a lot of lore, or a sport like baseball with very rich statistics.

Lore maximization reaches its apotheosis in the ideas of the late Dr Ray Peat, who has views so esoteric that even aficionados disagree on them. Some of my most enjoyable evenings have come from advancing Peatist views to uncomprehending, spluttering audiences. He advises consuming sugar, especially in the form of ice cream or orange juice, to speed up the metabolism, or even eating dessicated beef thyroid.

Though Peatism was pure affectation, it shined a light on what was really happening. I didn’t really believe in all the supplements I was taking – I just treasured the esoteric dietary knowledge, like a kind of modern-day druid. This blinded me to the fact that a big share of my research was confirmation bias.

But there was a more profound problem. People like the wise Stuart Ritchie and my colleague Saloni Dattani had been telling me for ages that science was overloaded with complete nonsense, which I accepted on an intellectual level but had not really absorbed into my intuitions. My feeling had always been that we could still draw conclusions if we had a big enough pile of papers. But now I have come to believe that something like 90 percent of research is nearly valueless.

Subscribe now

Just as Peatism was undermining my emotional investment in supplementation, an intellectual justification for supplement scepticism appeared in the form of a blog post by Milky Eggs. The average paper in nutrition science is so bad, because of the usual range of poor research practices ranging from fraud to p-hacking, that even large bodies of research papers can have not just the wrong magnitude of effect, but the wrong sign. It is surprisingly easy to produce dozens of papers showing something false, and what’s more, there is a bandwagon effect, and people do it all the time.

The proposed mechanism through which amino acid glycine extends life is by inhibiting methionine (another amino acid)’s effect on a particular signalling pathway. But with evidence as weak and inconsistent as it is today, how can we be sure that any random amino acid we supplement is not really functioning as a methionine?

This isn’t to say that there are never beneficial supplements for normal omnivores, but I am now suitably chastened. Silly old Stuart, I always said – why does he think that everyone, just by ‘eating a balanced diet’ (me: chortle, snigger), will have maxed out their ability to absorb micronutrients? ‘Piss it oot’ indeed. Well, I’m afraid that Stuart has had the last laugh.

Ben Southwood is an editor at Works in Progress.

item.title: How should armies fight?
item.description: A review of The Arms of the Future by Jack Watling.
item.content:encoded:
By Pieter Garicano

This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print. If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here.

Occasionally a book gets the next war right. In 1937, Heinz Guderian argued in Achtung – Panzer! that tanks should concentrate in armored formations, that those formations were best controlled by radio, and that their purpose was to break through enemy lines and fight beyond them. In 1940, Guderian used a German tank corps to punch through French defenses and trap almost two million Allied soldiers.

Jack Watling may have written another book like that. Watling, a British military analyst who works closely with the Ukrainian general staff, published The Arms of the Future in 2023. It argues that three forces define war today: the reach of sensors, the range of weapons, and the precision of munitions. All three are improving and have made the way armies previously fought impossible.

Sensors come in many forms. They include cameras mounted on consumer drones, commercial satellites and ground surveillance radars. Some listen: an acoustic sensor carried by a single soldier can identify a tank from ten kilometers away. Others use lasers to detect heartbeats or electronic emissions to locate a soldier making a phone call.

Once the sensors have found a target, modern munitions can destroy it from much further away. Eighty years ago, heavy artillery firing at sixteen kilometers missed by an average of fifty meters. In tests today, heavy artillery firing at seventy kilometers misses by an average of just two meters. Other weapons like rocket artillery and kamikaze drones regularly hit targets at twice that range.

This is a problem for the way modern militaries, including Western ones, fight. Generals try to combine surprise and concentration: secretly assembling a large group of soldiers and tanks and quickly overpowering the enemy. But both are impossible if a radar operator can spot vehicles assembling from fifty kilometers away and artillerymen start hitting them minutes later.

Already, grouping vehicles in Ukraine within a few tens of kilometers of the front line often gets them destroyed. As sensors and munitions improve, this ‘gray zone’ keeps growing, reaching far into what used to be the rear. The countryside, traditionally the place where generals like to maneuver, has become extremely dangerous: any concentration of forces is detected and then destroyed from a distance. How, then, should armies fight?

The first option soldiers have is to make themselves not worth shooting. They can do this by dispersing and hardening – digging deep holes and sitting in them. This is a great tactic when defending, but ensures that any attack they mount will be piecemeal and bloody.

Their second option is to withdraw to the places where cameras cannot see them and shells struggle to kill them: cities. To the modern soldier, the urban environment is like a warren of tunnels, full of shelters that preserve mobility. They require specialized troops to attack, and even then, fighting is difficult. But an army that ignores the countryside will soon find itself surrounded and cut off, and sitting in a city doesn’t solve the problem of attacking the enemy.

Their third option, and Watling’s preference, is to try to restore movement and surprise by fighting the sensors themselves. The ideal army of the future combines small groups of highly mobile soldiers that target enemy sensors and deploy their own with heavy artillery that support them from further back and specialized assault units that fight over cities and other strongpoints. The hope is not to revive the long offensives of Guderian’s tanks but to create a brief window in which troops can assemble and take a single objective without being spotted and destroyed.

The Arms of the Future came out three years ago. Since then, the war in Ukraine has evolved along the lines Watling predicted. Most Ukrainian soldiers live underground, sometimes for months at a time and hundreds of meters from the nearest friendly unit. They avoid movement whenever possible and, when forced to hold ground, prefer towns and cities, as they did at Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka. A Ukrainian battalion commander tells Watling: ‘I don’t need reinforcements, I need buildings to fight from.’ The attacking Russians, who have no holes to sit in, no cities to shelter in, and can neither concentrate nor achieve surprise, are suffering astonishing losses.

That doesn’t mean successful attacks have become entirely impossible. Some Ukrainian units, like the Third Assault Brigade, are learning to fight as Watling would want, targeting enemy sensors before grouping together and rushing forward. These attacks appear to be working, and may keep the battlefield moving for a while. But they will succeed only as long as they manage to keep blinding the enemy. If the cameras keep improving and the shells keep flying, that too may stop being an option.

item.title: The trouble with serendipity
item.description: Many scientific discoveries didn’t happen the way you think.
item.content:encoded:
By Saloni Dattani

Saloni Dattani explores accidental discoveries in history, and comes away learning that scientists’ lives were messier than she expected.

This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print. If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here.

People love accidental discoveries. Penicillin’s discovery by Alexander Fleming is a classic example. Fungal spores wafted in through an open window, fell onto a plate of bacterial colonies, and dissolved them. Another is Louis Pasteur’s discovery of a chicken cholera vaccine, the second vaccine ever developed. After Pasteur left a broth overexposed to oxygen, it went stale. But he ran out of fresh broth, so used it anyway to study the effects of an infection, and found, surprisingly, that it protected the chickens. Or how about the discovery of X-rays? Wilhelm Röntgen was working with a cathode ray tube in a dark room when he suddenly noticed a screen glowing nearby, even though he’d wrapped the tube in cardboard.

Subscribe now

Though they’re great stories, I’ve come to believe none of them happened that way. Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, and the story is just a hypothesis. Pasteur was extremely secretive as well, and forbade his family from making his notes and letters public after his death. His grandson, however, did, and after poring over their contents, historians have found that the key experiments were done deliberately by Pasteur’s then-assistant Émile Roux while Pasteur was away for his daughter’s wedding.

And what about Fleming? His first paper describing penicillin in 1929 never says where the spores came from. Of course, it’s hard to see how he could have known, given they would have been microscopic. But Fleming first told the window story in an interview in 1945, sixteen years after his first report, and his colleagues testified the window was ‘seldom if ever opened’. They weren’t able to replicate the discovery as he described, either: penicillin would have needed to be present on the plate before the bacteria grew, because it blocks bacteria from building their cell walls, rather than killing them once they’ve grown.

Subscribe to print

Several people have tried to work out what really happened. Fleming’s would-be biographer Ronald Hare made dozens of attempts and found just one reliable way to reproduce the discovery that fit the facts. The spores, he argues, were an unusually productive strain; came from the lab of a fungal researcher on the floor below, rather than the window; settled on the plate roughly when Fleming seeded it with bacteria; Fleming forgot to incubate it; and all this happened during a cold spell in the summer that let the mold grow before the bacteria. Hare noted how much more serendipitous this sequence of events was: ‘the odds against the occurrence of the phenomenon become almost astronomical’, though he ultimately believed it. While writing this column, I read through many of his notes and letters archived at the Wellcome Library and have come to agree with his view: Hare was exceedingly careful in corroborating the events from multiple people and sources from the time.

Part of the reason I find the popular stories fascinating is because it’s jarring to realize how little they’re based on. I do expect some stories of accidental discovery will survive the test of time. In medicine, for example, it’s fairly common to test a drug for one disease and find, unexpectedly, that it works for another: colchicine was used for centuries to treat gout before it was found effective against cardiovascular disease, and sildenafil (Viagra) was being tested for angina when its more famous effect was noticed. Side effects are difficult to predict.

Subscribe now

But I wonder why the popular versions have survived so long. Maybe they’re more enjoyable? They’re certainly easier to recount than the other explanations, which are convoluted. A fungal spore floating through an open window to reveal a world-changing antibiotic is a far better dinner party story than a meandering one involving several more coincidences you’ve probably already forgotten. Or the stories make scientists feel just like us: anyone can stumble upon a discovery, and then the challenge is merely to... spend years turning it into something useful?

‘Chance favors only the prepared mind’, as Pasteur put it. I think there’s something to it: the brilliance of these scientists isn’t necessarily in their initial discoveries, but in seeing their potential and doing something with them. Edward Jenner, for example, wasn’t the first to notice that cowpox infections protected against smallpox, but he documented it thoroughly and popularized the method, spreading smallpox vaccination worldwide.

But what bothers me is that calling these discoveries accidents is sometimes the opposite of reality. Pasteur and Roux, for example, carried out hundreds of experiments to find reliable methods to create new vaccines – the popular framing is actively misleading and diminishes their work.

My friend Niko McCarty recently dug into other famously serendipitous discoveries in biology, such as those of green fluorescent protein and nanopore sequencing, and explained they came from systematic trial and error. He also describes the idea of ‘engineered serendipity’: in optogenetics, for example, ‘the key breakthrough came about because the inventors wrote down the exact requirements they were looking for [...] and then enumerated, or wrote down, all the ways they could possibly imagine to make this happen’. It makes me wonder if learning how they really happened could help understand how to make more discoveries systematically.

Yet I’m still left with questions. Why credit chance events instead of hard work? Why hide or burn your notebooks?

Messiness, mistakes, and privacy come to mind. But here’s another theory: competition and rivalry. Gerald Geison, a historian of Pasteur, suggests the method he ultimately used to develop chicken cholera vaccines was ‘remarkably simple’ and could be applied to other diseases too: ‘had he revealed immediately the method of attenuation through exposure to ordinary air, Pasteur might have faced a host of competitors in the search for other vaccines’. Pasteur was probably the best-paid scientist in France at the time, and sold his inventions commercially. His secrecy might have been rational: patents weren’t allowed on medicines in France then, so keeping the method secret would have helped him maintain his monopoly on producing them. Pasteur was so cagey that he didn’t allow his collaborators to take notes, took his notebooks with him when he traveled, and published his methods (without much detail) only months after announcing his discoveries.

Subscribe to print

Meanwhile, Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays and had his notes burned after his death, had been in a long dispute with another scientist, Philipp Lenard. Lenard had spent years researching cathode rays before him, and shared his methods and discharge tube with Röntgen. Once Röntgen became famous, Lenard accused him of having robbed him of the discovery. That dispute, historians suggest, could have motivated the note-burning, but it’s hard to know without being able to read them. (Incidentally, Émile Roux, too, had his notes burned periodically, and it’s only because Pasteur’s were released that we know what happened at all.)

Science seems like it should be above the messiness. It’s an institution we’ve built to guard against our biases. But it’s also just people – who forget, hide their notebooks from their colleagues, burn their papers, and spend years fighting over who deserves credit. It’s shaped by rivalries, incentives, obsessions, and years of unglamorous work, most of which is forgotten. That, to me, makes it far more interesting than a story about an open window.

Saloni Dattani is an editor at Works in Progress.

item.title: The unfair edge of biotech hedge funds
item.description: It’s almost impossible to make money from investing in biotech, unless you know the right people.
item.content:encoded:
By Abhishaike Mahajan

This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print. If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here.

The notion of biotech hedge funds always felt a little strange to me. Yes, hedge funds are filled with clever people with clever ideas, like trading brick-and-mortar stocks based on satellite imagery showing how many cars are in their parking lots, but how are you going to trade on clinical trial results? Start up a lab? Whether drugs work in humans feels as unpredictable as anything else in biology. Maybe you can depend on the base rate of how often drugs for a particular disease area are approved, but everyone knows that already. Surely there are no dollar bills on the ground here waiting to be picked up.

And yet, hundreds of billions of dollars are managed by hedge funds and investment firms that specialize in biotech. The largest are Baker Brothers Advisors, Deerfield Management, and OrbiMed, each managing over $15 billion. Below them sit dozens more. How can these funds, some of which have been around for decades, possibly know more than the people doing the science?

Well, a surprisingly large number of clinical trial results are actually decently predictable by anyone willing to simply look. Some very expensive trials are run for seemingly no reason at all, all of which have failed incredibly badly in the past and have little reason to succeed in the future. LLMs may have replaced a decent chunk of the work here, but, in the past, hiring a small army of graduate students to compile information was table stakes for any self-respecting hedge fund. One of the most famous of the pack – RA Capital – has an entire division called ‘TechAtlas’ dedicated to the effort.

But we needn’t rely on LLMs or human ingenuity for this! Insilico Medicine has published a paper on inClinico, a platform that predicts Phase II clinical trial outcomes using embarrassingly simple inputs: ‘target choice’ features (whether this is a good drug for this disease, based on omics data and a biomedical knowledge graph) and ‘trial design’ features (like enrollment size, blinding, number of endpoints, patient age, location, and funder type). Their predictions, which were date-stamped and published on preprint servers before the trials read out, hit 79 percent accuracy across 14 resolved trials.

But then we arrive at the same problem as before: if it’s as easy as training a model or a human on what is essentially public information, how does anybody make money here?

Sometimes the answer is private information. The biotech investing industry spends enormous sums on paid consultations with expert networks. The business model is straightforward. An analyst at a biotech hedge fund wants to understand whether a particular clinical trial is likely to succeed. They pay an expert network $500 to $1,000 or more per hour to connect them with an individual who treats the disease in question, or who has run similar trials, or sits on advisory boards, or is otherwise an ‘expert’. The analyst asks questions, and the expert answers.

The stated purpose is to gain non-obvious insights. All of this is perfectly above board. There is no legal apparatus that prevents you from staring deeply into a clinician’s glassy eyes and asking them whether the trial’s endpoint is well chosen. There is nothing stopping you from taking their moment of hesitation as a sign of something worth trading on. It is a friendly conversation, and the SEC cannot prevent you from making friends.

This conversation also happens to be the same context in which the single largest insider trading transaction in American history occurred.

The main character is Mathew Martoma, who was a portfolio manager at SAC Capital Advisors, a hedge fund dealing in many areas, including biotech. In 2006, through one of the aforementioned expert networks – Gerson Lehrman Group – Martoma connected with Dr Sidney Gilman, a neurology professor at the University of Michigan who chaired the safety monitoring committee for bapineuzumab, an Alzheimer’s drug in clinical trials. Over two years, Martoma arranged dozens of paid consultations with Gilman. Based on Gilman’s optimistic reports about the trial’s progress, SAC built a position worth roughly $700 million in bapineuzumab’s two sponsoring companies. Then, in July 2008, Gilman learned the drug was failing. He told Martoma. Over the following days, SAC liquidated the entire $700 million position and went short. When the results were publicly announced later that month, SAC had netted $275 million in combined profits and losses avoided by selling the long holdings early.

Obviously, Martoma was convicted in 2014 of securities fraud. SAC Capital paid $1.8 billion in fines and pleaded guilty to fraud charges, and rebranded as Point72 Asset Management. Yes! That Point72!

How did they catch this guy anyway? The government, via an entity called FINRA, runs electronic surveillance on all shares traded on the NYSE, Nasdaq, and over the counter, including historical trading patterns. And they noticed something rather archetypical: someone held a massive long position, liquidated the entire thing, and then reversed to a short position all in the span of a few days, right before catastrophic news hit. FINRA flagged this to the SEC, which in turn alerted the FBI, which in turn pressured Gilman, who was 81, facing the end of his career, and potential prosecution, into cooperating in exchange for no jail time.

Now, an interesting question to ask is: could Martoma have gotten away with it? Probably not, given how egregious both his offenses were. But if you talk to people involved who invest in biotechnology, it seems that the thing that led to the Martoma prosecution never stopped in any meaningful sense. It went on before the case, and it has continued since. Expert consultations are more likely to be recorded now and people are more scared to say something incriminating; the SEC is not magic, but it has ruined enough lives to function as a deterrent at the explicit end of the spectrum.

But the game of increasingly subtle information extraction continues, and it is a game hard to enter for those outside of a hedge fund. You can only imagine how much this continues in entirely private, unrecorded conversations, between two friends who went to graduate school together, one who works as a scientist, and another who works in finance.

This all said: it would be unfair of me to malign the biotech hedge fund industry at large because of stories like this, which do genuinely represent edge cases. We can quibble about the relative utility of, say, nanosecond-faster trading, but it feels obviously correct that accurate pricing of biotech companies is a net good for the world. Good drug developers should get money, bad ones should not get money.

But for the most accurate players in this game, it also feels obvious that two things are true. One, that they are enormously prescient at seeing where the future may go in ways that are often opaque to even their peers – consider Baker Brothers’ twenty-year investment in Seagen, one of the first antibody-drug-conjugate companies, an investment which ended up converting $2 billion into $10 billion. And two, at least some of them are the beneficiaries of information that nobody else could ever reasonably have.

Abhishaike Mahajan is a columnist for Works in Progress and writes the blog Owl Posting.

item.title: How to make a lovable city
item.description: Camillo Sitte made the blueprint for beautiful cities. Here are his five principles.
item.content:encoded:
By Phoebe Arslanagić-Little

Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.

The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.

Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.

Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.

Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.

Share

Create enclosed spaces

The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.

While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.

The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.

Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.

London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.

An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.

Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.

Squares should not be too large

If a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).

Subscribe to print

Some of the world’s most famous squares are, in fact, far too large. St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, seen above, was designed by the famous artist Bernini, and it does indeed look impressive in drone footage. For human visitors, however, it is an exhausting place, overwhelming without being impressive. The Basilica looks small and stubby, exactly the opposite of the desired effect. On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.

By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.

Symmetry is overrated

At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical plans, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.

Sitte rejected this, believing that symmetrical spaces do not necessarily feel harmonious at ground level, and that asymmetry is not generally disharmonious at all. The pictures above show the perfectly symmetrical Place Vendôme in Paris. Seen from a satellite, it is visually striking and certainly neater than an irregular space. Its chamfered plan supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. Pedestrians, however, generally do not stand at the exact point at which the objective balance of the buildings is reflected in their field of vision: the various points and angles from which they do experience it may even make it feel quite awkward.

Above is the Piazza delle Erbe, a market square in Verona. This ‘square’ has an odd shape, an elongated and slightly wonky pentagon. Nobody is likely to model perfume bottles on it. But at human level, this does not matter as pedestrians can never take in all five sides at once, and so its irregular form is barely even visible. For the most part, the irregularities are ‘seen only on paper’, and to the extent they are visible, they are not experienced as imperfections. Sitte argued that they in fact serve to subtly arouse visual interest, and also create happy recesses that can host resting places, statues, or other public art.

Subscribe to print

Move monuments to the edges

If you were putting an ornament in your living room, you would be very unlikely to stand it in the middle of the carpet. It would get in the way, break up the space, and might well look lost and isolated. Nor would you place it in front of one of the room’s main features, like the fireplace. It would block the view of the fireplace, and the fireplace would be a disagreeably busy backdrop. Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.

Sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.

This was implicitly understood in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, and Sitte illustrates his book with examples from all three periods. Above, for example, is the Piazza della Signoria in Florence. The numerous statues line the sides of the square, leaving the center free for people to pass through or mill about. This is advantageous for the statues too: Michelangelo’s David (today a replica, since the original was moved indoors) stands out splendidly against the plain masonry walls of the Palazzo Vecchio.

Later planners became fascinated by the apparent neatness of centering statues. Above is the Victoria Memorial in London. The Memorial stands on the main axis of the Mall, blocking the view of Buckingham Palace behind it. This is not advantageous for the Memorial either, whose outline clashes confusedly with the complex detailing of the building. If you search through pictures of the Memorial, you will notice that most photographers picture it from an awkward oblique angle, the least bad way to capture both the monument and the central pavilion of the palace.

Isolating statues against the sky is not much better. A bronze cast of David was later placed on the Piazzale Michelangelo, at the center of a wide square with stunning views over Florence. The statue is enormous, over five meters tall, but it looks strangely miniaturized in its location. Sitte remarked that contemporary tourists often came away with the drastically false impression that it was life-sized. We judge size partly by comparison, and when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess. This is why the backdrop of a wall can make sculpture look bigger and grander by providing a constant visual key.

In Sitte’s view, the plain edge of a small square was not only an acceptable site for a statue, but the best one. Sitte disliked museums, which he called ‘art prisons’, and thought that only people with a ‘special mental preparation’ could enjoy art under their ‘morbid influences’. The Sittesque city would be one that teemed with art, but woven into the urban fabric as an adornment of ordinary civic life.

Share

Buildings need context

Sitte’s view on buildings was similar. Nineteenth-century architects tended to place major public buildings in the middle of squares, judging that this gave them greater dignity. Sitte thought this ‘pedantic, futile modern practice’ destroyed the square and squandered the opportunity to frame the public building with vernacular architecture. He pointed out that many historic cities were in fact designed along the lines he proposed. Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four. Only six were freestanding, two of them modern churches of expatriate Protestant communities.

The most striking examples of this arose when nineteenth-century governments actually demolished the vernacular buildings that surrounded historic monuments. This practice, often known by its French name dégagement, was surprisingly common: nineteenth-century planners thought that it displayed the monuments better. It provides a useful experiment on the effect of freestanding versus adjoined monumental architecture.

For example, Notre Dame Cathedral was formerly approached through a narrow street called the Rue Neuve Notre Dame. The street was demolished by the government planner Haussmann in the nineteenth century to create the Parvis Notre-Dame, a large square that the cathedral still faces today. Haussmann intended to improve the view of the cathedral, but the effect is the opposite. The vernacular fabric formed a visual frame, defining and concentrating views onto the facade. It provided scale, making the cathedral look larger by contrast to the ordinary buildings around it. It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.

Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.

Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.

The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte

The Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.

Subscribe to print

Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid plan, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.

But Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.

Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.

Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.

Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.
